verses.zh: 我对你们举荐我们的姊妹非比；她是坚革哩教会中的女执事。
verses.en: Now I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is a servant[NOTE:1] of the church in Cenchrea,
notes: Or “deaconess.” It is debated whether διάκονος (diakonos) here refers to a specific office within the church. One contextual argument used to support this view is that Phoebe is associated with a particular church, Cenchrea, and as such would therefore be a deacon of that church. In the NT some who are called διάκονος are related to a particular church, yet the scholarly consensus is that such individuals are not deacons, but “servants” or “ministers” (other viable translations for διάκονος). For example, Epaphras is associated with the church in Colossians and is called a διάκονος in Col 1:7, but no contemporary translation regards him as a deacon. In 1 Tim 4:6 Paul calls Timothy a διάκονος; Timothy was associated with the church in Ephesus, but he obviously was not a deacon. In addition, the lexical evidence leans away from this view: Within the NT, the διακον- word group rarely functions with a technical nuance. In any case, the evidence is not compelling either way. The view accepted in the translation above is that Phoebe was a servant of the church, not a deaconess, although this conclusion should be regarded as tentative.
verses.commentary:
16:1 "I commend to you" Verses 1-2 function as a letter of recommendation for deaconess Phoebe. She
probably carried Paul's letter to Rome. There are several other examples of these letters of introduction or
recommendation in the NT (cf. Acts 18:27; 1 Cor. 16:3; 2 Cor. 3:1; 8:18-24; and Phil. 2:19-30).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEACONESS

▣ "Phoebe" Her name meant "bright" or "radiant."

16:1

NASB, NKJV
"who is a servant of the church"

NRSV
"a deacon of the church"

TEV
"who serves the church"

NJB, Peshitta
"a deaconess of the church"

REB
"a fellow-Christian"

This is the term diakonos. It is an ACCUSATIVE SINGULAR FEMININE form.
It is the Greek term for minister/servant. It is used

- of Christ in Rom. 15:8; Mark 10:45

- of Paul in Eph. 3:7; Col. 1:23,25

- of deacons in Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:11

There is evidence in both the NT and early post-biblical church writings for the office of
deaconess. Another example of women in local church ministry in the NT is "the widows' roll" of the Pastorals
(cf. 1 Tim. 3:11; 5:3-16).

- The RSV, Amplified, and Phillips translations have "deaconess" in Rom. 16:1.

- The NASB and NIV have it in the footnotes.

- The NEB has "who holds office."

All believers are called, gifted, full-time ministers (cf. Eph. 4:12). Some are called to leadership
ministry roles. Our traditions must give way to Scripture! These early deacons and deaconesses were servants, not executive boards.

M. R. Vincent, Word Studies, vol. 2, pp. 752 and 1196, says that the Apostolical
Constitutions, dating from the late second or early third century, makes a distinction between the duties
and ordination of female church helpers.

- deaconesses

- widows (cf. 1 Tim. 3:11; 5:9-10)

- virgins (cf. Acts 21:9 and possibly 1 Cor. 7:34)

These duties involved

- caring for the sick

- caring for those physically persecuted

- visiting those in prison for the faith

- teaching new believers

- assisting in baptism of women

- some overseeing of female church members

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEACONESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN MINISTRY

▣ "church" See SPECIAL
TOPIC: CHURCH (EKKLĒSIA)

▣ "Cenchraea" This was one of two seaports of Corinth. This one was on the eastern side (i.e. Aegean Sea, cf.
Acts 18:18).

verses.zh: 请你们为主接待她，合乎圣徒的体统。她在何事上要你们帮助，你们就帮助她；因她素来帮助许多人，也帮助了我。
verses.en: so that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints and provide her with whatever help she may need from you, for she has been a great help to many, including me.
verses.commentary:
16:2 "that you receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy" This is an AORIST MIDDLE
[deponent] SUBJUNCTIVE of prosdechomai, which means "to receive kindly as a guest"
(cf. Phil. 2:29). Paul trusted this lady and wanted the church to receive her and help her on his behalf. The
very fact that he needed to say this shows the cultural climate of the first century in the Mediterranean world
(except for Macedonia).

▣ "saints" This term means "holy ones." It describes not only a believers' position in Jesus
(i.e. positional sanctification), but also hopefully their godly lives, progressively characterizing their new
holy position in Christ (i.e. progressive sanctification). The term
"saint" is always in the PLURAL except once in Philippians (Phil. 4:21) and even there it is
in a corporate sense. To be a Christian is to be part of a believing community, a family, a body. The modern
church in the west has depreciated this corporate aspect of biblical faith!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SAINTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: SANCTIFICATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

▣ "help her in whatever matter she may have need of you" There are two SUBJUNCTIVES.

- The first, paristēmi (AORIST ACTIVE), means "to stand by so as to aid."

- The second, chrēzō (PRESENT ACTIVE), means "to help with whatever is required"
(cf. 2 Cor. 3:1).

- This referred to material provisions for itinerant ministers. This was the purpose of letters of recommendation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION

▣

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"has been a helper of many"

NRSV
"has been a benefactor of many"

TEV, REB
"for she herself has been a good friend to many people"

NJB
"has looked after a great many people"

This term, proistatis, is found only here in the NT. This could have referred to
physical or financial help. This word originally referred to a wealthy patroness. Since Phoebe was traveling
to Rome (cf. Rom. 16:1) and had helped many (cf. Rom. 16:2), this may be historically true of her.

verses.zh: 问百基拉和亚居拉安。他们在基督耶稣里与我同工，
verses.en: Greet Prisca and Aquila,[NOTE:1] my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,
notes: On Prisca and Aquila see also Acts 18:2, 18, 26; 1 Cor 16:19; 2 Tim 4:19. In the NT “Priscilla” and “Prisca” are the same person. Paul uses the name Prisca, while the author of Acts uses the diminutive form of the name Priscilla.
verses.commentary:
16:3 "Prisca and Aquila" Luke calls her "Priscilla." She is often named before her husband, which was
culturally very unusual (cf. Acts 18:18, 26; 1 Cor. 16:19; 2 Tim. 4:19). Possibly she was of Roman nobility
or the dominant personality of this couple. Both Paul and this couple were tent-makers or leather workers.
Paul calls them "fellow workers in Christ Jesus." He possibly heard of the strengths and weaknesses of the
Roman church from this couple.

SPECIAL TOPIC: AQUILA AND PRISCA/PRICILLA

verses.zh: 也为我的命将自己的颈项置之度外。不但我感谢他们，就是外邦的众教会也感谢他们。
verses.en: who risked their own necks for my life. Not only I, but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them.
verses.commentary:
16:4 "risked their own necks" This is an idiom from the term for an "executioner's axe." The Bible is
silent on what Paul meant by this phrase.

▣ "to whom not only do I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles" Paul was very
grateful for the friendship and active help of this couple. He even expands their service to "all the churches
of the Gentiles." What a sweeping affirmation and thanksgiving! It might refer to their encouraging and
informing ministry to Apollos (cf. Acts 18:24-28).

verses.zh: 又问在他们家中的教会安。问我所亲爱的以拜尼土安；他在亚细亚是归基督初结的果子。
verses.en: Also greet the church in their house. Greet my dear friend Epenetus,[NOTE:1] who was the first convert[NOTE:2] to Christ in the province of Asia.[NOTE:3]
notes: The spelling Epenetus is also used by NIV, NLT; the name is alternately spelled Epaenetus (NASB, NKJV, NRSV).
Grk “firstfruit.” This is a figurative use referring to Epenetus as the first Christian convert in the region.

Grk “Asia”; in the NT this always refers to the Roman province of Asia. The Roman province of Asia made up about one-third of modern Asia Minor and was on the western side of it. Asia lay to the west of the region of Phrygia and Galatia. The words “the province of” are supplied to indicate to the modern reader that this does not refer to the continent of Asia.
verses.commentary:
16:5 "the church" This refers to a people, not a building. The term meant "the called out ones." In the
Greek OT, the Septuagint (LXX), this term was used to translate the Hebrew term qahal, translated
"congregation." The early Church saw themselves as the natural successors and fulfillment of the OT phrase
"congregation of Israel," and not a sectarian splinter group.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH

▣ "that is in their house" The early Christians met in homes (cf. Rom. 16:23; Acts 12:12;
1 Cor. 16:19; Col. 4:15 and Philemon 2). Church buildings did not appear until the third century
A.D.

▣ "Epaenetus" This man's name means "praised."

▣ "who is the first convert" This is also said of the household of Stephanas in 1 Cor. 16:15.

▣ "from Asia" This referred to the Roman province which made up the western one-third of modern
Turkey.

verses.zh: 又问马利亚安；她为你们多受劳苦。
verses.en: Greet Mary, who has worked very hard for you.
verses.commentary:
16:6 "Mary, who has worked hard for you" Nothing is known about this person. She may have been a
missionary from the Roman church. So many wonderful, godly believers are unknown to us but well known to God.

verses.zh: 又问我亲属与我一同坐监的安多尼古和犹尼亚安；他们在使徒中是有名望的，也是比我先在基督里。
verses.en: Greet Andronicus and Junia,[NOTE:1] my compatriots[NOTE:2] and my fellow prisoners. They are well known[NOTE:3] to the apostles,[NOTE:4] and they were in Christ before me.
notes: Or “Junias.” sn The feminine name Junia, though common in Latin, is quite rare in Greek (apparently only three instances of it occur in Greek literature outside Rom 16:7, according to the data in the TLG [D. Moo, Romans [NICNT], 922]). The masculine Junias (as a contraction for Junianas), however, is rarer still: Only one instance of the masculine name is known in extant Greek literature (Epiphanius mentions Junias in his Index discipulorum 125). Further, since there are apparently other husband-wife teams mentioned in this salutation (Prisca and Aquila [v. 3], Philologus and Julia [v. 15]), it might be natural to think of Junia as a feminine name. (This ought not be pressed too far, however, for in v. 12 all three individuals are women [though the first two are linked together], and in vv. 9-11 all the individuals are men.) In Greek only a difference of accent distinguishes between Junias (male) and Junia (female). If it refers to a woman, it is possible (1) that she had the gift of apostleship (not the office), or (2) that she was not an apostle but along with Andronicus was esteemed by (or among) the apostles. As well, the term “prominent” probably means “well known,” suggesting that Andronicus and Junia(s) were well known to the apostles (see note on the phrase “well known” which follows).
Or “kinsmen,” “relatives,” “fellow countrymen.”

Or “prominent, outstanding, famous.” The term ἐπίσημος (episēmos) is used either in an implied comparative sense (“prominent, outstanding”) or in an elative sense (“famous, well known”). The key to determining the meaning of the term in any given passage is both the general context and the specific collocation of this word with its adjuncts. When a comparative notion is seen, that to which ἐπίσημος is compared is frequently, if not usually, put in the genitive case (cf., e.g., 3 Macc 6:1 [Ελεαζαρος δέ τις ἀνὴρ ἐπίσημος τῶν ἀπὸ τής χώρας ἱερέων “Eleazar, a man prominent among the priests of the country”]; cf. also Pss. Sol. 17:30). When, however, an elative notion is found, ἐν (en) plus a personal plural dative is not uncommon (cf. Pss. Sol. 2:6). Although ἐν plus a personal dative does not indicate agency, in collocation with words of perception, (ἐν plus) dative personal nouns are often used to show the recipients. In this instance, the idea would then be “well known to the apostles.” See M. H. Burer and D. B. Wallace, “Was Junia Really an Apostle? A Re-examination of Rom 16.7,” NTS 47 (2001): 76-91, who argue for the elative notion here.
Or “among the apostles.” See discussion in the note on “well known” for these options.
verses.commentary:
16:7 "my fellow prisoners" Modern scholars are not certain to what imprisonment this referred. Paul
suffered much for his faith (cf. 2 Cor. 4:8-11; 6:4-10; 11:25-28). He was in prison at Philippi, Caesarea,
Rome, and probably other places as well (cf. Ephesus, 1 Cor. 15:32; 2 Cor. 1:8).

▣ "Junias" This name could be MASCULINE or FEMININE, which must be
determined by accent marks. There are Greek manuscript variations.

- "Iounian," is found in MSS א, A, B, C, D, F, G and P, but with no accent mark

- The accented FEMININE form is found in MSS B2, D2, and 0150.

- The early papyrus manuscript P46 and some Vulgate and Coptic translations, as well as the Greek texts used
by Jerome, have "Ioulian" which is FEMININE.

Some scholars think that this was a scribal error. This FEMININE form does occur in
Rom. 16:15.

It is possible that the two persons named in Rom. 16:7 (i.e. Andronicus and Junias) were

- two Jewish believers who were imprisoned with Paul

- a brother and sister

- a husband and wife

If it is FEMININE and if the phrase "the apostles" referred to a wider use of that
term than "the Twelve," then this was a lady apostle. See
SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTLE

It is also interesting that the spelling "Junias" has not been found anywhere in Roman
literature or inscriptions, but the name "Junia" was very common. It was a Roman family name. For more
information on women in ministry see Women Leaders and the Church, by Linda L. Belleville, pp. 188
footnote 42.

▣

NASB
"who are outstanding among the apostles"

NKJV
"who are of note among the apostles"

NRSV
"they are prominent among the apostles"

TEV
"they are well known among the apostles"

NJB
"to those outstanding apostles"

REB
"who are eminent among the apostles"

Peshitta
"well-known among the apostles"

This can refer to the Twelve, if so these two were well known to the church in Rome, or to a wider group
of ministers known as "apostles" (cf. Acts 14:4, 14; 18:5; 1 Cor. 4:9; Gal. 1:19; Phil. 2:25; 1 Thess. 2:6).
The context implies this wider usage, as in Eph. 4:11, but the DEFINITE ARTICLE implies the
Twelve.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEND (APOSTELLŎ)

▣ "who also were in Christ before me" This obviously means they were saved and active in Christ's
service before Paul's Damascus road experience (i.e. Acts 9).

verses.zh: 又问我在主里面所亲爱的暗伯利安。
verses.en: Greet Ampliatus, my dear friend in the Lord.
verses.commentary:
16:8-16 The names in this section are unknown to scholarship. They are beloved of God and Paul, but
their names and service are not recorded in the NT or early Christian literature. What is remarkable is that
there is a mixture of

- common slave names

- noble Roman

- Jewish family names

There are both men and women. There are wealthy freedman and itinerant preachers. There are foreigners
from Persia. All barriers are down in the church of Jesus Christ (cf. Rom. 3:22; 10:12; Joel 2:28-32
[Acts 2:14-21]; 1 Cor. 12:11; Gal. 3:28; Eph. 2:11-3:13; Col. 3:11)! The gospel is an open door for all who will respond.

16:8 "Ampliatus" This name, like Prisca and Junia, was a well known Roman family name.

▣ "my beloved in the Lord" The term "beloved" is used by God the Father for Jesus the Son at His
baptism in Matt. 3:17 and at His transfiguration in Matt. 17:5. It may be a title from the Servant Songs of Isaiah
(cf. Matt. 12:18, quoting Isa. 42:1). However, Paul uses it to address believers (cf. Rom. 1:7; 16:8,9; 1 Cor. 4:14,17; 15:58;
Eph. 6:21; Phil. 2:12; Col. 4:7,9,14; 1 Tim. 6:2; Philemon 16).

verses.zh: 又问在基督里与我们同工的耳巴奴，并我所亲爱的士大古安。
verses.en: Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my good friend Stachys.
verses.commentary:
16:9 "Urbanus" The name means "city dweller" or "city bred."

▣ "in Christ" This is a repeated phrase, along with "in the Lord," throughout this chapter. These
Christian workers were all part of one family, one Savior.

▣ "Stachys" This is a rare name which means "ear" (of grain). Archaeology has found this name
associated with Caesar's family.

verses.zh: 又问在基督里经过试验的亚比利安。问亚利多布家里的人安。
verses.en: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.
verses.commentary:
16:10 "the approved in Christ" This idiomatic phrase refers to one who had gone through trials and
remained faithful.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK TERMS FOR TESTING, #1

▣ "those of the household" Some scholars speculate that this phrase refers to slaves in the
domestic service of Aristobulus and not family members, and the same is true of the phrase in Rom. 16:11,
"those of the household of Narcissus."

▣ "of Aristobulus" Some scholars (Lightfoot) speculate that this was the brother of Herod
Agrippa I (who in Acts 12 had the Apostle James killed). If so, it shows how the gospel had begun to permeate
this royal Idumean family.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FAMILY OF HEROD THE GREAT

verses.zh: 又问我亲属希罗天安。问拿其数家在主里的人安。
verses.en: Greet Herodion, my compatriot.[NOTE:1] Greet those in the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.
notes: Or “kinsman,” “relative,” “fellow countryman.”
verses.commentary:
16:11 "Herodian" This may have been a slave of the family of Herod.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HERODIANS

▣ "those of the household of Narcissus" This may have referred to the well known servant of
Emperor Claudius. If so, it shows how the gospel had begun to permeate the Roman royalty.

verses.zh: 又问为主劳苦的土非拿氏和土富撒氏安。问可亲爱为主多受劳苦的彼息氏安。
verses.en: Greet Tryphena[NOTE:1] and Tryphosa, laborers in the Lord. Greet my dear friend[NOTE:2] Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.
notes: The spelling Tryphena is also used by NIV, NKJV, NLT; the name is alternately spelled Tryphaena (NASB, NRSV).
Grk “Greet the beloved.”
verses.commentary:
16:12 "Tryphaena" This name means "dainty."

▣ "Tryphosa" This name means "delicate." They were possibly sisters, even twins.

▣ "worked hard" The term has the connotation of labor "to the point of exhaustion."

▣ "Persis" This means "Persian woman."

verses.zh: 又问在主蒙拣选的鲁孚和他母亲安；他的母亲就是我的母亲。
verses.en: Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother who was also a mother to me.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “and his mother and mine.”
verses.commentary:
16:13 "Rufus" This name means "red" or "red-headed." There was an apparently well known Rufus in Rome
(cf. Mark 15:21). Whether he can be identified with this person is uncertain but surely possible.

▣

NASB
"a choice man in the Lord"

NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta
"chosen in the Lord"

TEV
"that outstanding worker in the Lord's service"

NJB
"a chosen servant of the Lord"

REB
"an outstanding follower of the Lord"

This is literally "the elect one." Here the term relates not only to God's call, but also to
his lifestyle service. His mother also treated Paul with great affection.

verses.zh: 又问亚逊其土、弗勒干、黑米、八罗巴、黑马，并与他们在一处的弟兄们安。
verses.en: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters[NOTE:1] with them.
notes: Grk “brothers.” See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:13.
verses.commentary:
16:14 "Hermes" This is the name of the Greek god of good luck. It was a very common slave name of the first
century Greco-Roman world.

verses.zh: 又问非罗罗古和犹利亚，尼利亚和他姊妹，同阿林巴并与他们在一处的众圣徒安。
verses.en: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the believers[NOTE:1] who are with them.
notes: Grk “saints.”
verses.commentary:
16:15 "all the saints" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SAINTS

verses.zh: 你们亲嘴问安，彼此务要圣洁。基督的众教会都问你们安。
verses.en: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verses.commentary:
16:16 "holy kiss" There is no early written evidence of who kissed who, or when, or where. In the synagogue,
whose form of greeting was continued in the church, the men kissed men on the cheek and the women kissed the
women (cf. 1 Cor. 16:20; 2 Cor. 13:12; 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14). This act of greeting became a problem
within the church because it was misunderstood by unbelievers and, therefore, was stopped in some churches,
although Justin Martyr mentions it in the second century.

verses.zh: 弟兄们，那些离间你们、叫你们跌倒、背乎所学之道的人，我劝你们要留意躲避他们。
verses.en: Now I urge you, brothers and sisters,[NOTE:1] to watch out for those who create dissensions and obstacles contrary to the teaching that you learned. Avoid them!
notes: Grk “brothers.” See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:13.
verses.commentary:
16:17-18 This warning seems to break into the context unexpectedly. However, Paul may have included it as
a contrast to godly itinerant ministers. There is a list in Rom. 16:17-18 of what these false teachers were
doing.

- they stirred up divisions

- they put hindrances in the believer's way

- they taught in opposition to the instruction the church had given (i.e. apostalic truth)

- they were serving their own base appetites

- they were deceiving the hearts of unsuspecting people by their smooth, flattering talk

This list is not related to the weak and strong believers of Rom. 14:1-15:13.

▣ "turn away from them" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE. This is a recurrent theme
(cf. Gal. 1:8-9; 2 Thess. 3:6,14; 2 John 10). This was a form of church discipline. These were apparently in the house churches
of Rome.

verses.zh: 因为这样的人不服事我们的主基督，只服事自己的肚腹，用花言巧语诱惑那些老实人的心。
verses.en: For these are the kind who do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By their smooth talk and flattery they deceive the minds[NOTE:1] of the naive.
notes: Grk “hearts.”
verses.commentary:
16:18

NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB
"their own appetites"

NKJV, Peshitta
"their own belly"

NJB
"their own greed"

This is literally "bellies" (cf. Phil. 3:19; Titus 1:12). The false teachers turned
everything to their own base interests.

▣ "by their smooth and flattering speech" False teachers are often physically attractive and have
dynamic personalities (cf. Col. 2:4). They are often very logical in their presentations. Beware! Some
possible biblical tests to identify false teachers are found in Deut. 13:1-5; 18:22; Matt. 7; Phil. 3:2-3,
18-19; 1 John 4:1-3.

▣ "they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE
denoting ongoing deception. These apparently new or naive believers were vulnerable ("inexperienced in evil"). This
same problem is mentioned in 1 Timothy and Titus.

verses.zh: 你们的顺服已经传于众人，所以我为你们欢喜；但我愿意你们在善上聪明，在恶上愚拙。
verses.en: Your obedience is known to all and thus I rejoice over you. But I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.
verses.commentary:
16:19 "the report of your obedience has reached to all" This is referred to in Rom. 1:8. This is one of
Paul's hyperboles. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 22, 110-117, 121, 133, 181.

▣ "be wise. . .in what is good, and innocent in what is evil" This reflects the teaching of Jesus
(cf. Matt. 10:16; Luke 10:3).

verses.zh: 赐平安的　神快要将撒但践踏在你们脚下。愿我主耶稣基督的恩常和你们同在！
verses.en: The God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.
verses.commentary:
16:20 "the God of peace" This is a wonderful title for God (cf. Rom. 15:33; 2 Cor. 13:16; Phil. 4:9;
1 Thess. 5:23 and Heb. 13:20). See note at Rom. 15:5.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT)

▣ "will soon crush Satan under your feet" This is an allusion to Gen. 3:15. The believer's
relationship with the Messiah gives them victory over evil (cf. 1 John 5:18-20). This is an awesome promise and
responsibility. In this context Satan epitomizes the confusion and division caused by false teachers which
causes the church to lose its Great Commission focus. Behind false teachers is the demonic (cf. 1 Cor. 10:20; Eph. 6:10-18)!
The gospel, however, dispels darkness and evil for those who embrace it and live it. For a good book on this subject
see Three Crucial Questions About Spiritual Warfare, by Clinton E. Arnold.

With my new understanding of a Partial Preterism perspective, this could refer to

- the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 (cf. Rev. 2:9,13; 17:3,8-17). For more information see my
commentaries on

- Matthew 23-24

- Revelation Introduction

- the destruction of Rome

- in the death of Nero (A.D. 68) and the empire wide chaos that followed (cf. Rev. 16:10-12;
Tacitus, The Histories 3.83)

- in the fall of the empire in A.D. 476 (some Partial Preterists, Rev. 13-19)

verses.zh: 与我同工的提摩太，和我的亲属路求、耶孙、所西巴德，问你们安。

notes: Grk “kinsmen, relatives, fellow countrymen.”
verses.commentary:
16:21-23 These verses are a post script (NJB). Paul's co-workers at Corinth sent their greetings.

16:21 "Lucius" This could have been

- Luke the physician (cf. Col. 4:14), or possibly an idiom for "highly educated one"

- Lucius of Cyrene (cf. Acts 13:1)

- an unknown Christian

▣ "Jason" This is possibly the Jason in whose house Paul stayed at Thessalonica (cf. Acts 17:5-9).

▣ "Sosipater" This man is possibly the Sopater of Berea in Acts 20:4.

verses.zh: 我这代笔写信的德提，在主里面问你们安。
verses.en: I, Tertius, who am writing this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verses.commentary:
16:22 "I, Tertius, who write this letter" NJB calls this a "second postscript." Paul used a scribe (amanuensis)
to write his letters (cf. 1 Cor. 16:21; Gal. 6:11; Col. 4:18; 2 Thess. 3:17). I think Paul had poor eye sight (see note at 2 Cor. 12:7)
and could not write the small, tight script needed to preserve space on a sheet of papyrus or leather scroll (cf. Gal. 6:18)!

verses.zh: 那接待我、也接待全教会的该犹问你们安。
verses.en: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus the city treasurer and our brother Quartus greet you.[NOTE:1]
notes: Most mss (D [F G 629 without “Jesus Christ”] Ψ [630] 1175 1241 1505 1881 M al) include here 16:24 “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.” Other mss (P 33 104 365) include the verse after 16:27. The verse is entirely lacking in P46, 61 א A B C 81 1739 2464 co. The strength of the external evidence, combined with uncertainty in other mss over where the verse should be located and the fact that it is a repetition of v. 20b, strongly favors omission of the verse. The present translation follows NA28 in omitting the verse number, a procedure also followed by a number of other modern translations.
verses.commentary:
16:23 "Gaius" This could have been

- Gaius Titius Justus of Acts 18:7

- Gaius of Derbe (cf. Acts 19:29; 20:4; 1 Cor. 1:14)

- the Gaius of 3 John 1

▣ "host to me and the whole church" This was the hospitality needed in the early church (cf. Rom. 12:13;
1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:8; Heb. 13:2; 1 Pet. 4:9). Some believers with resources allowed the traveling Christian ministers to room
and board. Some, as this man, also opened his home to be the meeting place for gathered events. House churches were
the norm for over two hundred years.

▣ "Erastus, the city treasurer" He is also mentioned in Acts 19:22; 2 Tim. 4:20. He had an
itinerant ministry connected to Paul.

▣ "Quartus" This name in Latin means "fourth." He was possibly the brother of Tertius, which in
Latin means "third" (cf. Rom. 16:22).

verses.zh: 城内管银库的以拉都和兄弟括土问你们安。
verses.commentary:
16:24 This verse is not present in the early Greek manuscripts, P46,61,
א, A, B, C, and 0150. It is found in some Greek manuscripts after Rom. 16:23
and others after Rom. 16:27. It is obviously not original with Paul. It is omitted in the NASB, NRSV, TEV and NJB
translations. The UBS4 rates its omission as "certain" (A). It is an attempted close to the letter
and is related to the problem of the closing doxology being at the end of Romans 14; 15; and 16 in various
ancient Greek texts.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

verses.zh: 惟有　神能照我所传的福音和所讲的耶稣基督，并照永古隐藏不言的奥秘，坚固你们的心。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that had been kept secret for long ages,
notes: There is a considerable degree of difference among the mss regarding the presence and position of the doxology of 16:25-27. Five situations present themselves from the ms tradition. The doxology is found in the ancient witnesses in three separate locations: (1) here after 16:23 (P61 א B C D 81 365 630 1739 2464 al co), (2) after 14:23 (Ψ 0209vid M), or (3) after 15:33 (P46). The situation is further complicated in that some of the mss have these verses in two places: (4) after 14:23 and after 16:23 (A P 33 104); or (5) after 14:23 and after 15:33 (1506). The uncertain position of the doxology might suggest that it was added by later scribes. But since the mss containing the doxology are so early and widespread, it almost certainly belongs in Romans; it is only a question of where. Further, the witnesses that omit the doxology are few: F G 629 Hiermss. (And of these, G has a blank space of several lines large enough for the doxology to belong there.) Only two positions (after chapter 14 only and at the end of the letter only) deserve particular notice because the situation of the mss showing the doxology in two places dates back to the 5th century. Later copyists, faced with the doxology in two different places in the mss they knew, may have decided to copy the doxology in both places, since they were unwilling to consciously omit any text. Because the textual disruption of the doxology is so early, TCGNT 472 suggests two possibilities: either (1) that Paul may have sent two different copies of Romans—a copy lacking chapter 16 and a copy with the full text of the epistle as we now have it, or (2) Marcion or some of his followers circulated a shortened form of the epistle that lacked chapters 15 and 16. Those mss that lacked chapters 15-16 would naturally conclude with some kind of doxology after chapter 14. On the other hand, H. Gamble (The Textual History of the Letter to the Romans [SD], 123-32) argues for the position of the doxology at 14:23, since to put the doxology at 16:25 would violate Paul’s normal pattern of a grace-benediction at the close of the letter. Gamble further argues for the inclusion of 16:24, since the mss that put the doxology after chapter 14 almost always present 16:24 as the letter’s closing, whereas most of the mss that put the doxology at its traditional position drop 16:24, perhaps because it would be redundant before 16:25-27. A decision is difficult, but the weight of external evidence, since it is both early and geographically widespread, suggests that the doxology belongs here after 16:23 and that v. 24 is not authentic. For a full discussion, see TCGNT 470-73.
verses.commentary:
16:25-27 This is one sentence in Greek. This benediction can be found in ancient Greek manuscripts,
both at the end of Romans 14 and Romans 15, as well as here. This context is a recapitulation of the major themes of
the book possibly written in Paul's own hand.

Some believe that this doxology may have been

- the cover letter for the cyclical letter of Ephesians

- for those on the way to Rome because

- Paul had never visited Rome, yet he says hello to twenty-six people

- Romans 16 is the first mention of false teachers

- this doxology appears in the Greek manuscripts at several different places

It is also possible that Paul made two copies, Romans 1-14 to Rome, Romans 1-16 to Ephesus.
Usually these assertions are answered by

- the fact that many of these early Christian workers traveled

- the fact that no Greek manuscript of Romans is without Romans 16

- the possibility that false teachers are implied in Rom. 14:1-15:13

16:25 "to Him who is able" This is another wonderful title for God used three times in the NT
(cf. Eph. 3:20; Jude 24). See partial list of the descriptive NT titles for God at Rom. 15:5.

Notice how God establishes believers.

- Paul's gospel presentation

- the preaching about Jesus Christ

- the revealing of God's eternal plan of salvation which had been kept secret (mystery)

Believers are enabled by the knowledge of the gospel. This gospel has now been made available to
all!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

▣ "the mystery" God has a unified purpose for mankind's redemption that even preceded the fall
(cf. Genesis 3). Hints of this plan are revealed in the OT (cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6; and the universal
passages in the Prophets). However this full agenda was not clear (cf. 1 Cor. 2:6-8). With the coming of Jesus
and the Spirit it begins to become more obvious. Paul used the term "mystery" to describe this total
redemptive plan (cf. 1 Cor. 4:1; Eph. 2:11-3:13; 6:19; Col. 4:3; 1 Tim. 1:9). However, he uses it in several
different senses.

- A partial hardening of Israel to allow Gentiles to be included. This influx of Gentiles will work as
a mechanism for Jews to accept Jesus as the Christ of prophecy (cf. Rom. 11:25-32).

- The gospel was made known to the nations, which are all included in Christ and through Christ
(cf. Rom. 16:25-27; Col. 2:2).

- Believers' new bodies at the Second Coming (cf. 1 Cor. 15:5-57; 1 Thess. 4:13-18).

- The summing up of all things in Christ (cf. Eph. 1:8-11).

- The Gentiles and Jews are fellow-heirs (cf. Eph. 2:11-3:13).

- Intimacy of the relationship between Christ and the Church described in marriage terms (cf.
Eph. 5:22-33).

- Gentiles included in the covenant people and indwelt by the Spirit of Christ so as to produce
Christlike maturity, that is, restore the marred image of God in fallen humanity (cf. Gen. 6:5, 11-13;
8:21) of God in man (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 5:1; 9:6; Col. 1:26-28).

- The end-time Anti-Christ (cf. 2 Thess. 2:1-11).

- An early church summary of the mystery is found in 1 Tim. 1:16.

was foretold by the OT prophets. The establishment of a NT church made up of believing Jews and Gentiles was
always God's plan (cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6; Jer. 31:31-34).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ROMANS 16: 1-27

- Notice that all of the women in this closing section were fellow-workers with Paul in the gospel
(cf. Phil. 4:3):

- Phoebe in Rom. 16:1

- Prisca in Rom. 16:3

- Mary in Rom. 16:6

- Junia (or Junias‒if so it was a man) in Rom. 16:7

- Tryphaena and Tryphosa in Rom. 16:12

- Persis in Rom. 16:12

- "his mother" in Rom. 16:13

- Julia in Rom. 16:15

- "his sister" in Rom. 16:15

Be careful of dogmatism in the area of women in ministry. All believers are called, gifted (cf. 1 Cor. 12:7,11),
full-time ministers (cf. Eph. 4:12).

In this list we have a woman deacon, Phoebe, and a possible woman apostle, Junia (cf. Joel 2:28;
Acts 2:16-21). It is difficult to know how to handle this issue biblically because of the seemingly paradoxical
statements of Paul such as 1 Cor. 11:4-5 compared with 14:34 and 1 Timothy 2:8-15. See my exegetical notes
on each of these passages online.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN MINISTRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN KEEP SILENT

- Notice the possible racial backgrounds of these names

- believing Jews: Aquila, Prisca, Andronicus, Junias, Mary (some MSS have Mariam)

- Roman noble family names: Prisca, Ampliatus, Apelles, Narcissus, Julia, Philologus

- Jewish noble family names: Aristobulus, Herodion

Paul ministered with women from several cultural backgrounds.

- This chapter can be outlined as

- verses 1-16 are Paul's personal greetings

- verses 17-20 are his closing warnings against false teachers

- verses 21-23 contain the mission team's greetings from Corinth

- The discussion of Romans 16 in the Tyndale New Testament Commentary by F. F. Bruce is very
helpful. If you are interested in a detailed study of the names found in this chapter, read pages
266-284.

- There is some doubt about where Paul's letter to the Roman church closes. A closing prayer appears
several times at the end of

- Romans 14

- Romans 15 (MS P46)

- Romans 16, in the ancient Greek manuscripts

However, the traditional close of Rom. 16:25-27 appears in MSS P61, א, B, C and D
as well as the Greek text used by Clement of Rome (A.D. 95). The UBS4 gives
the traditional conclusion (vv. 25-27) a "C" rating, meaning the committee could not decide if it was original.

Verse 24 does not appear in the older Greek manuscripts, P46, P61,
א, A, B, C, nor the Latin Vulgate or the Greek text used by Origen of Alexandria. The
UBS4 rates its omission as "B" (almost certain).

For a full discussion of the variants see Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, pp. 533-540.
